text.text: However, from the perspective of language acquisition, it can be helpful to consider only those morphemes which could be analysed from the perspective of a child learning the language.
Before applying automated morphemisers to the corpus, it was necessary to establish a set of theory-driven principles against which individual morpheme counts could be validated.
The four overriding principles are repeated here, as well as in the main paper.
Table S2 acted as a reference and guide for application of the rules.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">S2</ref> acted as a reference and guide for application of the rules.

text.text: (1) Principle of non-analysability: a word should not be broken into smaller constituent morphemes if a child would not be able to identify the constituent parts (e.g., men = [man] + [plural], but the internal vowel change is non-obvious to a child).

(2) Principle of non-productivity: a word should not be broken into smaller constituent morphemes if those morphemes are not used in active word building processes (e.g., in a child's understanding, the -let in bracelet would be unlikely to produce necklet as a synonym for necklace).

(3) Principle of non-semantic transparency: a word should not be broken into smaller morphemes if the word is not meaningfully composed of smaller constituent parts (e.g., red cannot be broken into smaller meaningful parts; a compound word such as rainbow does not obviously mean the combination of the rain and bow according to a child's understanding of the two words).
(4) Principle of cross-linguistic equivalence: the logic of these three principles should apply across languages, even though they may not apply equally to individual translation equivalents.
Note that this means that morpheme counts will be higher or lower for expressions with similar meanings in different languages.
This is a natural feature of multilingualism and forms part of the parent's linguistic repertoire that they may deploy flexibly when translanguaging with their child.

Set-Phrases / Lexicalised expressions.
Some expressions required more consideration: a lot/a bit/a while vs. alot/abit/awhile.

These are grammatical expressions which are more frequently occurring in everyday life than the other compound words, and frequent words are subject to variation at a much higher rate than infrequent words (cf. Bybee, 2002; Pierrehumbert, 2003).
text.formatted: These are grammatical expressions which are more frequently occurring in everyday life than the other compound words, and frequent words are subject to variation at a much higher rate than infrequent words (cf. <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Bybee, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Pierrehumbert, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: The lexicalized versions such as 'alot' are also frequently used in text messaging, the ubiquity of which has an influence on other forms of writing.

As a result, allowed transcribers to use their interpretation as to whether they perceived these words as being said with no temporal pause between syllables (as in 'alot') or with a temporal pause between syllables (as in 'alot').
Instances of these were not very prevalent within these recordings hence any effect of a judgement of 1 or 2 morphemes for 'alot' vs. 'a lot' (and related words) was likely negligible.

Ellipses.

The use of ellipses in BELA was to indicate 1) interrupted speech, i.e., partial words (e.g., the ele...) and 2) complete words that trailed off (e.g., the elephant...) or 3) an interruption that was later resolved in the next utterance.
In the literature, partial words were usually excluded from the MLU computation (and would be scored as 0; e.g., Miller, 1981) whereas whole words were included (and scored as 1).
text.formatted: In the literature, partial words were usually excluded from the MLU computation (and would be scored as 0; e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Miller, 1981)</ref> whereas whole words were included (and scored as 1).

text.text: In terms of automatic language processing, there was no available way to automatise the checking of the ellipses to see which condition it fell under.
Thus, we made two counts: scoring all elided words as 0 or 1 to examine whether it would make a difference in MLU computation.
There was a significant difference in the median of utterances when all elided words were considered 1 (i.e., all considered whole words even if they were actually partial words).
In the interest of not excluding parents who often trailed words off in their speech, we factored into our model to count all elided words as 1.

Over 4 years, the Principal Investigator (the last author) had a core team of 7 full-time lab members at any given point, with at least 2 each who could speak Chinese, Malay or Tamil (NB: for Tamil, it was more typically 1 full-time staff member, 1 senior part-time student transcriber with sometimes an additional junior part-time student transcriber or intern).
There were 20 part-time student transcribers in the transcription team at any given point (there were 40 at its peak and 79 members in total throughout the 4 years).
Over the years, the student transcriber team was made up of 79 English, 60 Mandarin, 9 Malay and 10 Tamil speakers.
Data cleaning.

Following transcription, data pre-processing for metrics such as word-and morpheme-counts were developed by manually pre-processing a small number of files to establish a data-driven approach to processing, based on ground truth data and linguistic theory.

First, we selected 2% of the recordings (8 of 415) to be checked and segmented manually into words and morphemes (by the first author) and by extant automated morpheme processors (by the third author).
The two authors did this independently of the other before coming together in the first discussion to determine a set of pre-processing rules.

Utterances containing 'next', 'next page' and related phrases embedded in them proved to be tricky, as it was sometimes unclear whether it was a directive to the researcher (e.g., next page please) or it was one but it was said as a sentence to the child (e.g., okay next please let's find out ).

Hence, we operationalised this as follows: a) Exclude any utterance containing only 'next' or 'next page' b) Include directives to child to say 'next page', e.g., can you say next please?, let's say next, next please BABYNAME said, let's go to the next page then, okay it's going to change next page okay change c) Include questions to child about story flow, e.g., what happens next?, want to see what's on the next page?, okay next please let's find out, okay let's find out next please, next page what did he... uh next page what did he do?

d) Include utterances using 'next' for location and time, e.g., next time you can tell your teacher, what's next to the duck?, monkey go next okay e) Exclude clear administrative sentences, e.g., next (page/one/picture/slide) (please), turn (page) (please), (so/yes) (okay/alright/right) (then) next f) Check the addressee using prosody in mixed content with administrative sentences and keep content words, e.g., nice okay next, happy alright next, happy yes okay next page, got lightning again so next please
Thus, we followed a sequential order of pre-processing the recordings so that only text relevant to the narrative task was analysed for counts of words and morphemes.

During the development of theory-driven principles, manual coders were tasked with checking the outputs of automated morphemisers, and creating master-lists of textual exceptions, to be integrated into subsequent morphemising passes, which were again checked for consistency, until the automated morphemisers agreed with human coders' judgement.

The procedure was straightforward for Mandarin Chinese and Malay, took a few rounds of iterative refinement for English, and was not possible for Tamil (due to inability of the automated morphemisers to handle the informal transcriptions of the local variety), resulting in fully manual morphemising for Tamil language text in the corpus.
